title: The Educated Barbarian: Book of Five Rings analysis (part. 4)
summary: Part 4 of his reading of Musashi's Book of Five Rings, starting the Water Book. He applies Musashi's lines to lifting: absorb and apply knowledge rather than read or imitate it, lift in a calm, determined, repeatable state of mind instead of hyped rage, keep body and spirit in harmony, don't overreact to bodily signals, and treat good bracing posture as an everyday posture.

claims.claim: Musashi says the Way cannot be fully explained in words but can be grasped intuitively; the Way is how you live your life as a warrior, and it lies within you.
Intuition is not magic: like animal instinct it is biologically ingrained and triggered by cues you notice consciously or not; he recommends the book The Gift of Fear on this.
The Book of Five Rings will feel empty on the first few reads because its knowledge must be read between the lines intuitively; you find in it the wisdom you look for.
Information you don't apply is worthless: reading a two-hour paper on biceps growth without training biceps is a waste of life; applying knowledge makes it your own and lets you pass it on.
Humans dominate because they pass knowledge orally and then through books rather than relying on instinct alone; sharing applied experience is how the species evolves.
Never imitate anyone in lifting; imitation is worse than memorizing because it colours your actions with idolatry. Make your own way.
Don't get angry or enter a trance to lift: it isn't replicable, it tires your adrenaline response, and you become dependent on that state of rage to perform.
Lift in a neutral, determined but calm state; PRs set in that state are easy to replicate day to day, while tension and stress can make you miss lifts.
As powerlifters say, your mood should not determine the day's performance: feeling bad doesn't mean your strength is gone, and if strength is low but spirit is high you should push through.
Body and spirit should be in harmony and neither should dictate the other; for anxious, hyperactive people the lesson is to learn to calm the spirit.
His reading of Musashi: aim for a calm spirit and an always active body; calm means focused and determined with no stray thoughts, not empty-minded.
Going to the gym over-hyped isn't sustainable daily and going in depressed and low-energy yields no gains; find the middle ground, as with most of life, since extremes rarely pay off long term.
Don't over-interpret your body's signals: a muscle twinge on a warm-up squat set shouldn't end the session or be treated as a serious disease, though it shouldn't be ignored either.
You are not your body; you are a mind using the body as an envelope, and you choose how to interpret what it does.
'A giant is no expert': athletes who were always bigger never had to learn technique, e.g. Shaquille O'Neal never developed a jump shot because he could just dunk.
Athletes who were small until about 15-16 and then had a growth spurt (e.g. Michael Jordan) tend to be better because they built skill while small and then got size: the best of both worlds.

Musashi's posture advice (shoulders lowered, buttocks not jutting out, strength in the legs, abdomen braced so you don't bend at the hips) matches good lifting posture: shoulders back and down for a straight thoracic spine and neutral neck, glutes squeezed, legs tight, abs braced.
If the hips shoot back on a squat or deadlift you lose glute and posterior-chain drive and overuse the lower back, which leads to injury.
Make your lifting stance your everyday stance: the universal bracing cues that protect joints under heavy load also prevent overuse injuries when held all day.
The reverse also holds: a rounded everyday posture carries into your bench, squat and deadlift and hurts both performance and injury resistance.
Calling something weak isn't calling it bad: the lateral raise is weak compared with the deadlift but still useful; you use strong and weak things for different purposes.
